title: How to Create AI Educational Infographics That Actually Teach
author: Phillip Alcock
summary: Phillip Alcock gives teachers a step-by-step method for getting AI image tools to produce infographics that really teach. His claim is that failures come from skipping two thinking steps before prompting: defining learning goals as drawable visual outcomes and sketching a spatial blueprint. The four stages are concept, learning goals, visual zones and prompt, followed by evaluation, one-change-at-a-time refinement and export. He worked through a photosynthesis example and says the same loop applies to the water cycle, long division or history timelines. The piece is practical and classroom-specific, aimed at teachers rather than general professionals.
points: Weak infographics come from prompting before defining goals and layout, not from weak AI tools.
Learning goals must be drawable visual outcomes, ideally four, mapping to a four-zone layout.
Structure should lead the prompt and style keywords should come later, using six components in a set order.
Judge outputs against the learning goals rather than aesthetics, and fix one prompt sentence at a time.
quotes: Most AI-generated educational infographics fail not because the AI is bad, but because the prompt skips two critical thinking steps. This tutorial teaches you those steps.
Aim for exactly four goals. Four maps cleanly to a four-zone layout. More than four and the image becomes cluttered. Fewer and you risk missing the concept’s core logic.

A learning goal for an infographic is not a topic heading. It is a specific thing your student should be able to say or point to after looking at the image for 30 seconds. The test is simple: could you draw it?

One warning worth repeating directly: do not start the prompt with style keywords. Structure comes first. Most failed AI infographic prompts open with “a beautiful, vibrant, detailed...” and then vaguely describe the topic. The AI fills in the gaps however it chooses. When you start with structure, you direct those choices instead.

Paste your prompt into your chosen AI image generator and generate the first image. When it comes back, resist the instinct to judge it on appearance. The question is never “does it look good?” It is always “does it teach all four goals?

Each fix targets one sentence in your prompt. That is deliberate. When you change multiple things at once, you lose track of what worked. Treat each iteration as a controlled experiment with one variable.

The framework does not change what AI can produce. It changes what you bring to the conversation. An image that teaches is built from the goals first. The prompt comes last. That sequence is the whole thing.
